claim: In serial compound stimulus (SCS) conditioning in mice, repeated presentations of sequential tone (CS1) and white noise (CS2) auditory stimuli immediately prior to an aversive event (US) produces freezing and flight responses to CS1 and CS2, respectively.
source: In serial compound stimulus (SCS) conditioning in mice, repeated presentations of sequential tone (CS1) and white noise (CS2) auditory stimuli immediately prior to an aversive event (US) produces freezing and flight responses to CS1 and CS2, respectively (Fadok et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fadok et al., 2017, which is prior published work.

claim: Recent work reported that freezing and flight responses in SCS conditioning reflect learned temporal relationships of CS1 and CS2 to the US.
source: Recent work reported that these responses reflect learned temporal relationships of CS1 and CS2 to the US (Dong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2019.

claim: Frequency and sound pressure levels, not temporal proximity to the US, are the key factors underlying SCS-driven conditioned responses.
source: However, we find that frequency and sound pressure levels, not temporal proximity to the US, are the key factors underlying SCS-driven conditioned responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: White noise elicits greater physiological and behavioral responses than tones even prior to conditioning.
source: Moreover, white noise elicits greater physiological and behavioral responses than tones even prior to conditioning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pupillometry and running wheel experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Stimulus salience is the primary determinant of behavior in the SCS paradigm.
source: Thus, stimulus salience is the primary determinant of behavior in the SCS paradigm, and represents a potential confound in experiments utilizing multiple sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, inferred from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Stimulus salience represents a potential confound in experiments utilizing multiple sensory stimuli.
source: Thus, stimulus salience is the primary determinant of behavior in the SCS paradigm, and represents a potential confound in experiments utilizing multiple sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative implication drawn from the study's findings about stimulus salience.

claim: Human studies indicate that the specific neural circuits engaged during prediction of event occurrence depend on which cognitive strategy is used to solve a particular task.
source: Human studies indicate that the specific neural circuits engaged during prediction of event occurrence depend on which cognitive strategy is used to solve a particular task (Breska and Ivry, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Breska and Ivry, 2018.

claim: Predatory imminence theory posits that prey animals initially freeze when predators are present at a distance, but then switch to flight if a predator becomes close enough.
source: As posited by 'predatory imminence theory', prey animals initially freeze (to avoid detection) when predators are present at a distance, but then switch to flight (escape) to avoid entrapment if a predator becomes close enough that avoiding detection is no longer possible (Blanchard and Blanchard, 1989; Blanchard et al., 1995; Bouton and Bolles, 1980; Fanselow, 1994; Fanselow and Lester, 1988; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature on predatory imminence theory.

claim: The form of both appetitive and aversive conditioned responses varies substantially according to the particular properties of a given conditioned stimulus, even when the same underlying construct has been learned.
source: However, the form of both appetitive and aversive conditioned responses is known to vary substantially according to the particular properties of a given conditioned stimulus, even when the same underlying construct has been learned (Holland, 1977; Holland, 1979; Holland, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holland's work from 1977, 1979, and 1980.

claim: All groups exhibited significantly greater motion during white noise than tone, irrespective of the order that these stimuli were presented during training.
source: As evident from the motion traces (Figure 1D–F), all groups exhibited significantly greater motion during WN than TN, irrespective of the order that these stimuli were presented during training (Figure 1J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-F and Figure 1J-L.

claim: As conditioning progressed, mice in all groups began to exhibit active responses to the white noise, including darting and jumping.
source: As conditioning progressed, mice in all groups began to exhibit active responses to the WN, including darting and jumping, behaviors quantified using an 'escape score' (Figure 1M–O, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1M-O and described in the methods.

claim: Freezing to the tone differed between paired Group 1 and gap Group 3 during conditioning.
source: Freezing to the TN differed between paired Group 1 (G1) and gap Group 3 (G3) during conditioning. Freezing to TN was higher in G1 than G3 (3-Way ANOVA on Day 2, G1 vs. G3, Main Effect of Stimulus (F(1,23) = 429.5, p<0.0001), Main Effect of Trial (F(4,92) = 5.083, p=0.001), Group X Stimulus Interaction, (F(1,23) = 27.51, p<0.0001); Follow-Up Two-Way RM ANOVA for freezing just to the tone stimulus, Main Effect of Trial (F(3.2, 75.9)=3.79, p<0.05), Main Effect of Group (F(1,23) = 6.41, p<0.05)).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing groups 1 and 3.

claim: Mice in the paired group exhibited robust acute freezing upon tone onset in a novel context, while mice in the gap group did not show significantly increased freezing.
source: Whereas mice in the gap group (G3 protocol) did not show significantly increased freezing between baseline and tone onset (p>0.05), mice in the paired group (G1 protocol) exhibited robust acute freezing upon tone onset (p<0.001)(Two-Way RM ANOVA, Main Effect of Stimulus (F(1,13) = 19.98, p<0.001), Stimulus X Group Interaction (F(1,13) = 5.492, p<0.05), Sidak's comparisons to determine which group drives the Main Effect of Stimulus).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Motion and escape score during white noise presentations differed between Group 1 and Group 3 during conditioning.
source: Third, motion and escape score during WN presentations differed between G1 and G3 during conditioning. Mice in G1 had higher motion to WN than G3 mice (3-Way ANOVA on Day 2, G1 vs. G3 Activity, Main Effect of Stimulus (F(1,23) = 69.89, p<0.0001), Main Effect of Group (F(1,23) = 11.75, p<0.01), Group X Stimulus Interaction (F(1,23) = 19.77, p<0.001); Follow-up Two-Way RM ANOVA for motion just to WN stimulus, Main Effect of Group (F(1,23) = 15.79, p<0.001)), and also had higher escape scores to the WN stimulus (3-Way ANOVA on Day 2, G1 vs. G3 Escape Score, Main Effect of Stimulus (F(1,23) = 67.85, p<0.0001), Main Effect of Group (F(1,23) = 15.98, p<0.001), Group X Stimulus Interaction (F(1,23) = 20.41, p<0.001); Follow-up Two-Way RM ANOVA for escape score just to WN, Main Effect of Group (F(1,23) = 18.25, p<0.001)).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing groups 1 and 3.

claim: Group 1 motion responses to white noise on day 2 were largest immediately following stimulus onset and decreased thereafter until US exposure.
source: Notably, G1 motion responses to WN on day 2 (Figure 1D) were largest immediately following stimulus onset and decreased thereafter until US exposure (paired t-test, average motion first two vs. last two seconds of CS2, trials 6, 7, p<0.01; trials 8, 9, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Imminence in the SCS paradigm does not appear to be determined by a cognitive process that uses cue order or hazard rate.
source: Thus, imminence in the SCS paradigm does not appear to be determined by a cognitive process that uses cue order or hazard rate, and reversing stimulus order does not reverse behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that reversing stimulus order does not reverse behavior.

claim: Reversing stimulus order does not reverse behavior in SCS conditioning.
source: Thus, imminence in the SCS paradigm does not appear to be determined by a cognitive process that uses cue order or hazard rate, and reversing stimulus order does not reverse behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from Figure 1.

claim: The minimal sound pressure levels that mice can reliably detect for 16 kHz tones is ~10 x lower (10 dB) than for 7.5 kHz tones (20 dB).
source: For example, the minimal sound pressure levels (SPL) that mice can reliably detect for 16 kHz tones is ~10 x lower (10 dB) than for 7.5 kHz tones (20 dB) (Koay et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koay et al., 2002.

claim: Pupil dilation and simple locomotor responses on the running wheel were significantly greater to white noise than tone in naive, unconditioned mice.
source: Surprisingly, we found that pupil dilation and simple locomotor responses on the running wheel were significantly greater to WN than TN (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Tone responses habituate with repeated presentations, whereas white noise responses do not.
source: In addition, comparison of the first three versus last three trials revealed that whereas TN responses habituate with repeated presentations, WN responses do not (Figure 2G–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-N.

claim: A 7.5 kHz CS presented at high SPL should be perceived as more imminent and elicit more escape than the exact same CS presented at low SPL.
source: A prediction of this model is that a 7.5 kHz CS presented at high SPL should be perceived as more imminent and elicit more escape than the exact same CS presented at low SPL.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model proposed by the authors, which is then tested experimentally.

claim: 7.5 kHz tones began to elicit escape behaviors in the paired group when CS2 ≥90 dB.
source: While predominantly freezing was observed at ≤85 dB, 7.5 kHz tones began to elicit escape behaviors in the paired group when CS2 ≥90 dB (Figure 3D,F,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, F, H.

claim: Escape scores for trials where CS2 ≥90 dB were significantly higher in group 1 (paired) than group 3 (gap).
source: Further, escape scores for trials where CS2 ≥90 dB were significantly higher in group 1 (paired) than group 3 (gap; Figure 3H,I): 2-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA, Main Effect of Trial (F (4, 92)=3.208, p<0.05), Main Effect of Group (F (1, 23)=4.613, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: Group 1 responses are at least in part influenced by perceived threat levels which are a function of conditioned fear, and are not simply a reflexive reaction to loud sounds.
source: This argues that group one responses are at least in part influenced by perceived threat levels which are a function of conditioned fear, and are not simply a reflexive reaction to loud sounds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of paired and gap groups in the SPL step test.

claim: At low SPL (40–45 dB), white noise elicited robust freezing and little to no escape behavior.
source: At low SPL (40–45 dB), WN elicited robust freezing and little to no escape behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the white noise SPL step test shown in Figure 3M-O.

claim: At higher SPL (≥60 dB), white noise escape responses were common and freezing was minimal during white noise presentations.
source: In contrast, at higher SPL (≥60 dB), escape responses were common and freezing was minimal during WN presentations (Figure 3M–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M-O.

claim: SCS fear conditioned tone and white noise stimuli elicit freezing or flight behavior according to the SPL magnitude at which they are presented.
source: Thus, SCS fear conditioned TN and WN stimuli elicit freezing or flight behavior according to the SPL magnitude at which they are presented.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SPL step test experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The threshold SPL in mice is ~100 x lower for 12 kHz than 3 kHz pure tones.
source: These frequencies were chosen as: a) the threshold SPL in mice is ~100 x lower for 12 kHz than 3 kHz pure tones (Koay et al., 2002);
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koay et al., 2002.

claim: 12 kHz is well separated from 17 to 20 kHz, a range that may be innately aversive in mice.
source: and b) 12 kHz is well separated from 17 to 20 kHz, a range that may be innately aversive in mice (Beckett et al., 1996; Blanchard et al., 1992; Cuomo et al., 1992; Evans et al., 2018; Mongeau et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on innately aversive frequencies in mice.

claim: Paired groups exhibited higher motion, less freezing, and more escape to the 12 kHz than 3 kHz CS, regardless of the order in which the stimuli were presented during training.
source: As conditioning progressed, paired groups exhibited higher motion, less freezing, and more escape to the 12 kHz than 3 kHz CS, regardless of the order in which the stimuli were presented during training (Figure 4E–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-M.

claim: Despite having no apparent intrinsic aversive valence, 12 kHz tones can elicit greater active threat responses than 3 kHz tones presented at equivalent SPL during SCS conditioning.
source: Thus, despite having no apparent intrinsic aversive valence, 12 kHz tones can elicit greater active threat responses than 3 kHz tones presented at equivalent SPL during SCS conditioning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the two-tone SCS conditioning experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Audio frequency properties strongly influence the defensive behaviors elicited by SCS fear conditioned auditory stimuli.
source: In conclusion, we found that audio frequency properties strongly influence the defensive behaviors elicited by SCS fear conditioned auditory stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data from multiple experiments.

claim: Escape behaviors were most potently triggered by stimuli that contain frequencies to which mouse hearing is most sensitive, an effect that was independent of the order in which auditory stimuli were presented during learning.
source: Escape behaviors were most potently triggered by stimuli that contain frequencies to which mouse hearing is most sensitive, an effect that was independent of the order in which auditory stimuli were presented during learning.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data from multiple experiments.

claim: Pure tones that elicit freezing at typical experimental sound pressure levels can promote conditioned escape when presented at higher levels.
source: In addition, pure tones that elicit freezing at typical experimental sound pressure levels can promote conditioned escape when presented at higher levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the SPL step test experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The probability and intensity of escape behaviors to innately threatening visual stimuli in mice scale with visual stimulus salience.
source: This would appear to be similar mechanistically to how mice respond to innately threatening visual stimuli, where the probability and intensity of escape behaviors scale with visual stimulus salience (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2018.

claim: All species have a particular range of frequencies that they hear well (i.e. which are audible at 10 dB); stimuli outside of this range may need to be presented at substantially higher SPL in order to be efficiently detected.
source: Psychophysical studies have demonstrated that all species have a particular range of frequencies that they hear well (i.e. which are audible at 10 dB); stimuli outside of this range may need to presented at substantially higher SPL in order to be efficiently detected.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge in psychophysics and auditory perception.

claim: The 10 dB threshold includes frequencies ranging from ~5–40 kHz in rats.
source: For example, whereas the 10 dB threshold includes frequencies ranging from ~5–40 kHz in rats, this range is very narrow in mice and limited to frequencies close to 16 kHz (Heffner and Heffner, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 2007.

claim: The 10 dB threshold range is very narrow in mice and limited to frequencies close to 16 kHz.
source: For example, whereas the 10 dB threshold includes frequencies ranging from ~5–40 kHz in rats, this range is very narrow in mice and limited to frequencies close to 16 kHz (Heffner and Heffner, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 2007.

claim: C57BL/6J mice undergo hearing-loss induced plasticity that by 5 months of age results in loss of responsivity to high frequency tones (>20 kHz) with concomitantly enhanced behavioral sensitivity to middle (12–16 kHz) but not low (4–8 kHz) frequency stimuli.
source: For example, C57BL/6J mice undergo hearing-loss induced plasticity that by 5 months of age results in loss of responsivity to high frequency tones (>20 kHz) with concomitantly enhanced behavioral sensitivity to middle (12–16 kHz) but not low (4–8 kHz) frequency stimuli (Carlson and Willott, 1996; Willott et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carlson and Willott, 1996 and Willott et al., 1994.

claim: Rats emit and respond defensively to alarm vocalizations near 20 kHz.
source: Moreover, certain frequencies may be innately aversive in rodents: rats emit and respond defensively to alarm vocalizations near 20 kHz (Beckett et al., 1996; Blanchard et al., 1992; Cuomo et al., 1992),
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beckett et al., 1996; Blanchard et al., 1992; and Cuomo et al., 1992.

claim: 17–20 kHz ultrasonic sweeps can elicit robust freezing and flight behaviors in mice.
source: and 17–20 kHz ultrasonic sweeps can elicit robust freezing and flight behaviors in mice (Evans et al., 2018; Mongeau et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2018 and Mongeau et al., 2003.

claim: White noise stimuli may be uniquely salient to mice under conditions of impending potential threats due to recruitment of dedicated defensive circuits tuned to innately threatening auditory stimuli.
source: White noise stimuli, which are both aperiodic and include 17–20 kHz frequencies, may thus be uniquely salient to mice under conditions of impending potential threats due to recruitment of dedicated defensive circuits tuned to innately threatening auditory stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the properties of white noise and known responses to innately threatening frequencies.

claim: In conventional fear conditioning to a simple CS composed of a single auditory stimulus, significantly more flight behavior was evoked by a white noise CS than a tone CS.
source: Indeed, in conventional fear conditioning to a simple CS composed of a single auditory stimulus, significantly more flight behavior was evoked by a white noise CS than a tone CS (Fadok et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fadok et al., 2017.

claim: In the stress-enhanced fear learning (SEFL) model, exposure to inescapable shocks in the absence of auditory stimuli results in nonassociative freezing to white noise in a novel context on the following day.
source: For example, in the stress-enhanced fear learning (SEFL) model, exposure to inescapable shocks in the absence of auditory stimuli results in nonassociative freezing to white noise in a novel context on the following day (Perusini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perusini et al., 2016.

claim: Previous work provided behavioral and neurophysiological evidence that SCS fear conditioned tone and white noise stimuli acutely elicit distinct defensive states indicative of different points along the threat imminence continuum.
source: Previous work provided behavioral and neurophysiological evidence that SCS fear conditioned tone and white noise stimuli acutely elicit distinct defensive states indicative of different points along the threat imminence continuum (Fadok et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fadok et al., 2017.

claim: Defensive states in SCS conditioning track with the frequency and intensity of the conditioned stimuli, not order of CS presentation during learning.
source: We have found that these defensive states track with the frequency and intensity of the conditioned stimuli, not order of CS presentation during learning.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Threat imminence in the SCS model is determined primarily via the salience of threat-predictive auditory stimuli which, together with recent experience and current fear levels, determines the threshold for switching from freezing to flight.
source: This argues that threat imminence in this model is determined primarily via the salience of threat-predictive auditory stimuli which, together with recent experience (Mongeau et al., 2003) and current fear levels, determines the threshold for switching from freezing to flight.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, with a citation to Mongeau et al., 2003 for the role of recent experience.

claim: Another study reported that training with a 'reversed SCS' (white noise-tone-US) reverses the behaviors elicited (i.e. mice freeze to the WN but exhibit flight to the tones).
source: Our results contrast with those of another study (Dong et al., 2019), which reported that training with a 'reversed SCS' (white noise-tone-US) reverses the behaviors elicited (i.e. mice freeze to the WN but exhibit flight to the tones).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2019.

claim: Reversing the order of the white noise and tone stimuli during training had a quantitative effect, with white noise eliciting significantly less escape behavior when it preceded rather than followed the tone during training.
source: Although reversing the order of the white noise and tone stimuli during training did not qualitatively alter the type of behaviors elicited by the CSs, this switch did have a quantitative effect. Specifically, white noise elicited significantly less escape behavior when it preceded rather than followed the tone during training (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Compound stimuli which increase in salience from CS1 to CS2 may be more naturalistic and produce higher arousal levels and greater learning than the reverse order.
source: One potential explanation for this result is that compound stimuli which increase in salience from CS1 to CS2 are more naturalistic and produce higher arousal levels and greater learning than the reverse order.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Tonal stimuli which sweep from low up to high frequencies are rated by human observers as more alarming than high to low sweeps.
source: Indeed, tonal stimuli which sweep from low up to high frequencies are rated by human observers as more alarming than high to low sweeps (Catchpole et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Catchpole et al., 2004.

claim: Frequency upsweeps are associated with elevation of attention and arousal, whereas downsweeps are thought to have a calming effect.
source: Similarly, frequency upsweeps are associated with elevation of attention and arousal, whereas downsweeps are thought to have a calming effect (Owren and Rendall, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Owren and Rendall, 2001.

claim: Conditioned responses exhibited at the onset of a CS can differ qualitatively from those displayed near CS offset.
source: Finally, we note that conditioned responses exhibited at the onset of a CS can differ qualitatively from those displayed near CS offset (Holland, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holland, 1980.

claim: Male FVBB6 F1 hybrid mice (3–5 months of age, 25–30 g) were used for all experiments except those in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which used C57Bl/6J mice.
source: Male FVBB6 F1 hybrid mice (3–5 months of age, 25–30 g) were used for all experiments except those in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which used C57Bl/6J mice (JAX).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the subjects used in the study.

claim: All mice were singly housed beginning one week prior to and throughout training and testing.
source: All mice were singly housed beginning one week prior to and throughout training and testing, and maintained on a 12 hr reverse light/dark cycle with access to food and water ad libitum.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing housing conditions.

claim: All behavioral tests were conducted during the dark phase, beginning not before one hour of lights OFF and ending not later than one hour before lights ON.
source: All behavioral tests were conducted during the dark phase, beginning not before one hour of lights OFF and ending not later than one hour before lights ON.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the timing of behavioral tests.

claim: Darts were defined as rapid crossings preceded by immobility; jumps were defined as rapid movements in which all four paws left the floor.
source: Darts were defined as rapid crossings preceded by immobility; jumps were defined as rapid movements in which all four paws left the floor.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing how escape behaviors were defined and scored.

claim: Escape score was calculated by taking the difference in average motion index during CS versus the baseline for each trial, dividing this by 100, and then adding one point for each dart or two points for each jump observed during that particular stimulus and trial.
source: We therefore calculated an 'escape score' by taking the difference in average motion index (MI) during CS versus the baseline for each trial (i.e. the 10 s period preceding delivery of a CS), dividing this by 100, and then adding one point for each dart or two points for each jump observed during that particular stimulus and trial: escape score = (MICS – MIBL)/100 + 1 (for each dart) + 2 (for each jump).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing how the escape score was calculated.

claim: Mice used for pupillometry experiments had not previously received any type of conditioning nor been exposed to either tone or white noise stimuli.
source: Importantly, mice used for these experiments had not previously received any type of conditioning nor been exposed to either tone or white noise stimuli.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the naive status of mice used in pupillometry experiments.
